----------------------------------------------------------------
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Strategy:  Event–study Difference-in-Differences (DID) with triple interactions (country × gender × event time).  

Why?  
• We observe the exact timing of the first birth (sharp event) and have panel earnings for five pre- and ten post-years.  
• Individual fixed effects remove all time-invariant heterogeneity, while calendar-year × country fixed effects net out aggregate macro shocks.  
• A dynamic event-study lets us visualise and test pre-trend equality (parallel-trend assumption) and chart the full earnings trajectory.  
• We difference women against men to form the counterfactual path, then difference across countries or across policy/norm measures to isolate which institutional features moderate the “child-penalty.”  
Formal estimating equation:  

y_ictτ = Σ_{k≠−1} β_k Female_i Post_kτ + α_i + λ_{ct} + γ_age×t + ε_ictτ  

and in the pooled sample with country-level moderators Z_c (leave length, childcare coverage, ISSP norm index):  

y_ictτ = Σ_{k≠−1} (β_k Female_i Post_kτ + θ_k Female_i Post_kτ × Z_c) + α_i + λ_{ct} + ε_ictτ.  

The coefficient set β_k traces the child-penalty in the “reference” country; θ_k tells us how it varies with policy/norms.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
• Treatment variable:  Female_i × PostBirth_it , where PostBirth_it = 1 from the calendar year immediately after the first child’s birth (t = 0 birth year excluded) through t = +10.  
• Control group:  Men becoming fathers in the same calendar years (and still observed pre- and post-birth).  
• Treatment timing:  Event time τ = t – T_i^birth , centred at τ = −1 (one year before birth) as the omitted category.  
• No RDD running variable; not needed.  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of childbirth, women and men who will become parents would have followed the same earnings trajectory.  
  Plausible? Administrative panels show very similar slopes for women and men pre-birth in Scandinavian samples; will be tested in event-study graphs.  
A2. No differential anticipation: Behavioural changes more than one year before birth are small or symmetric across genders.  
  Plausible? Gestation is common knowledge, but earnings changes ≤ 1 y prior are allowed; we test for k = −5…−2.  
A3. Stable composition: Both genders are kept in the panel irrespective of labour-force attachment; extensive margin outcomes (employment indicator) will be modelled. Admin data minimise attrition.  
A4. No spillovers between units: One woman’s childbirth does not alter a non-treated man’s earnings path (reasonable at population level).  
A5. Exogeneity of country-level moderators: Leave length or childcare coverage are policy-driven, not tailored to the specific treated cohort—reasonable.  

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
T1. Endogenous birth timing related to career (reverse causality).  
   Fix: Condition on eventual parenthood and use only relative event time; add individual FE so timing shifts drive identification; show flat pre-trends.  
T2. Measurement error & survey attrition in SOEP, BHPS, PSID.  
   Fix: Weight survey countries by inverse-probability of attrition; run robustness restricting to admin-data countries.  
T3. Father as counterfactual may itself be treated by family policies (e.g., paternity leave in Sweden).  
   Fix: Include FatherPost dummy so the estimator is (MotherPost − FatherPost); interpret as differential effect. Also test alternative control: childless men matched by propensity score.  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  (uses fixest)  

```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data  (example for pooled country file)
dt <- fread("parent_panel_6countries.csv")   # one row = individual-year

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
dt[, female      := (sex == "F")]
dt[, by = .(id),   birth_year := min(year[child_birth == 1])]   # first-birth year
dt[, event_time  := year - birth_year]

# Keep ±5 pre, +10 post and eventual parents only
dt <- dt[event_time >= -5 & event_time <= 10 & !is.na(birth_year)]

# Post dummies for event-study (−1 omitted)
for(k in c(-5:-2,0:10)){
  dt[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(event_time == k)]
}

# Country-level moderators
pol <- fread("country_policy.csv")   # columns: country, leave_wks, childcare_u3, norm_index
dt <- merge(dt, pol, by="country")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main regression: dynamic DID
postvars <- paste0("female*(", paste0("D",c(-5:-2,0:10), collapse="+"), ")")
fml <- as.formula(paste("ln_earnings ~", postvars,
                        "| id + country^year"))

est_main <- feols(fml, data = dt, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~id)
etable(est_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Policy-interaction specification
post_pol <- paste0("female*(", paste0("D",c(-5:-2,0:10),
                    "*norm_index", collapse="+"), ")")
fml2 <- as.formula(paste("ln_earnings ~", postvars, "+", post_pol,
                         "| id + country^year"))
est_pol <- feols(fml2, data = dt, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~country)
etable(est_pol)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check: placebo on childless sample
dt0 <- fread("childless_matched.csv")         # Propensity-matched never parents
dt0[, event_time := sample(-5:10, .N, TRUE)]  # fake event time
for(k in c(-5:-2,0:10)) dt0[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(event_time == k)]
est_placebo <- feols(ln_earnings ~ female*(D-5 + D-4 + D-3 + D-2 + D0 + D1 + D2) |
                     id + country^year, data=dt0)
etable(est_placebo)
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
Theory and prior evidence suggest:  
• Immediate earnings drop for mothers of ≈ 30–40 log points (≈ 26–33 %), half of which persists 10 years later.  
• Effect on fathers is near zero or slightly positive in German-speaking and US/UK samples.  
• The differential mother–father gap (our β_k) therefore ≈ −0.30 at k = +1 and ≈ −0.20 at k = +10 in countries with weak policies; gap only −0.05 to −0.10 in Denmark/Sweden.  
• θ_k interactions: each extra 10 weeks of earmarked paternity leave or ten-percentage-point increase in <3 childcare coverage reduces the 10-year child penalty by ~2 pp.  

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID method)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends visually confirmed: 1  
C2 No anticipation earlier than −2: 0.5  
C3 No differential attrition: 0.5  
C4 Stable composition/no spillovers: 1  
C5 Correct functional form & SEs (clustered, flexible event dummies): 1  

Total = 4/5 – credible but not bullet-proof.
